covers.quote: Australian place names are proper nouns, written using standard Australian English.
Because of this reality, there may appear to be exceptions to the general rules given in this guide.

rules.violation_condition: An official Australian place name has the wrong lexical spelling or omits a hyphen or apostrophe belonging to its official spelling. Differences solely in capitalisation, diacritics, added punctuation or dual-name presentation belong to the more specific checks.
when: Use the official registered spelling, including established spellings that appear to depart from the general conventions.
This requirement concerns official names, not every name in a First Nations naming system.
Apply the address-specific presentation rules where they require a different postal presentation.
rules.why: G-4 retains the explicit spelling instruction; G-1 avoids using it as an umbrella that duplicates the specific style checks.

covers.quote: don’t use diacritical marks
loses any accent marks or diacritics

rules.violation_condition: A letter in an official Australian place name is outside the standard unaccented 26-letter alphabet, including a letter carrying an accent or other diacritical mark.
when: Applies to official Australian place names, including names adopted from other languages.
The alphabet restriction concerns letters, not spaces or expressly permitted punctuation.
Respect established official spellings that are exceptions to the general conventions.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4 combine the alphabet restriction and its repeated diacritic case into one allowed-letter check.

covers.quote: are not possessive
Hyphens and apostrophes can be part of an official name. They appear if they were part of the name of the person commemorated by the place name.

rules.specification: Use the registered name to resolve exceptions to ‘generally’. Treat the prohibition on possessives as a convention about the name itself, not a prohibition on grammatical possessives in surrounding prose.
rules.violation_condition: Punctuation is added within an official Australian place name without an official basis, including an apostrophe that incorrectly makes the name possessive.
when: Hyphens and apostrophes may belong to an official name when inherited from the name of the person commemorated.
Do not remove punctuation belonging to the official spelling.
Separators between the parts of an official dual name are assessed under the dual-name separator rule.
Punctuation belonging to the surrounding sentence is not punctuation within the name.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates possessive punctuation with the general punctuation check; G-3 records inherited punctuation as an exception.

rules.quote: When writing official dual names, use a spaced forward slash to separate the 2 parts of the name.
rules.violation_condition: The two parts of an official dual place name are not separated by a forward slash with a space on each side.
when: Applies when writing both parts of an official dual place name.
rules.why: G-1 and E-2 anchor this check to the instruction immediately above the dual-name examples, not the broad punctuation heading.

rules.quote: The order should be as written in the official name, which you can check in the Australian Place Names dataset.
rules.violation_condition: The two parts of an official dual place name appear in a different order from the registered official name.
when: Applies when writing both parts of an official dual place name.
rules.why: The grain test separates incorrect name order from an incorrect separator because they are distinct findings.

rules.quote: Write generic and plural terms in lower case.

covers.quote: Use standard shortened forms in addresses.

rules.violation_condition: A conventional address term is written in full where its standard shortened form is expected, or an address uses a non-standard shortening.

without punctuation

rules.quote: Do not add punctuation marks to these.

rules.violation_condition: A postcode appears before other content in the final delivery line of an Australian letter address rather than at its end.

A missing postcode is assessed under the required-components rule.
rules.why: The grain test separates an incorrectly positioned postcode from a missing address component.

rules.quote: The last line should contain the place name or post office of delivery, state or territory abbreviation and postcode.

when: Applies to Australian domestic letter addresses.
Either a place name or a post office of delivery satisfies the delivery-place component.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the alternative delivery-place forms within one required-components check.

rules.quote: If you are sending mail overseas, spell out all names in the address in full to avoid confusion.
rules.violation_condition: An address for mail being sent overseas contains an abbreviated or contracted name instead of its full form.
when: Applies when sending mail overseas.

rules.why: G-2 treats overseas delivery as the trigger; the explicit full-name requirement can produce a finding, unlike a mere permission.
